notes.label: Pactyes
notes.body: A Lydian whom Cyrus had trusted with the gold of conquered Lydia, and who used it to lead a revolt against the Persians. See the background panel below.

notes.label: Mazares
notes.body: A Median general in the service of Cyrus, sent to put down the Lydian revolt and to bring Pactyes back alive.

notes.label: Cyme
notes.body: A Greek city on the coast of Aeolis, in north-west Asia Minor (modern Turkey), and the largest of the Aeolian cities. Its people are the Κυμαῖοι, the Cymaeans.

notes.label: Branchidae
notes.body: The oracle of Apollo at Didyma, a little south of Miletus, named after the Branchidae, the family of priests who ran it.

notes.label: Ionians and Aeolians
notes.body: Two of the main groups of Greeks, each with its own dialect. The Ionian cities, Miletus the greatest of them, lay along the central coast of Asia Minor and its islands; the Aeolians lived further north, around Cyme and on Lesbos.

notes.label: Contrast (μέν ... δέ)
notes.quote: ὁ μὲν Πακτύης ... ὁ δὲ Μαζάρης
notes.body: The balanced construction sets the fugitive against his pursuer, so the reader sees the whole conflict in a single sentence.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Pactyes' fear is placed before his flight, which shows that terror of the Persians drives everything he does.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: Two verbs of movement side by side, so the reader sees a hurried escape.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: Cyme is named in both clauses, which shows the danger following Pactyes to the city that has taken him in.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Mazares gives orders and makes no request, so the reader feels the weight of Persian power.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: The only thing the Cymaeans decide is to pass the problem to the god, which shows how unwilling they are to take responsibility themselves.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Stressing the oracle's age gives it authority, so the reader expects its answer to be trustworthy.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.trans: all the Ionians and the Aeolians
notes.body: Two whole peoples are linked with τε καί, which shows how widely the oracle was respected.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: The journey to the oracle is covered by a single participle, so the story moves straight to the question.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: The Cymaeans ask how to keep the gods pleased, which suggests they care more about divine favour than about what is right.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.trans: as they asked ... a response came
notes.body: The answer arrives the moment they ask, which shows how clear and unhesitating the god is.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: The god's answer repeats Mazares' demand (line 79) almost word for word, so the reader is shocked that the god seems to side with the Persians.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.trans: to hand Pactyes over to the Persians
notes.body: The hard π, τ and δ sounds give the reply a clipped ring, which makes it sound blunt and final.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The Persians are the last words of the answer, so the reader is left thinking of the fate that awaits Pactyes.

questions: Why might Herodotus pause to tell us how old and how widely respected the oracle at Branchidae was, just before we hear its answer?
The god's reply (lines 85–86) uses almost the same words as Mazares' demand (line 79). What effect does that have on you as a reader?
What exactly do the Cymaeans ask the god in lines 83–84? Is it the question you would have asked in their position?

context.body:
Lydia was a rich kingdom in western Asia Minor, with its capital at Sardis. Its last king, Croesus, was defeated by Cyrus the Great of Persia in about 546 BC. Cyrus left a Persian, Tabalus, in command of Sardis, and gave a Lydian called Pactyes the job of collecting the gold of Croesus and the Lydians.

As soon as Cyrus had gone, Pactyes took the gold down to the coast, used it to hire soldiers, and besieged Tabalus in Sardis. Cyrus sent a Median general, Mazares, with an army to crush the revolt, with orders to bring Pactyes back to him alive. Pactyes did not wait for him: he fled to the Greek city of Cyme, and that is where this story begins.

A suppliant (ἱκέτης) put himself under the protection of a god, or of a more powerful person, by a recognised ritual: sitting at an altar or in a sanctuary, holding out a branch wound with wool, or kneeling and clasping the knees of the person he was begging. Zeus himself, as Zeus Hikesios, watched over suppliants, and to drag one away from an altar, or to hand one over to be killed, was a grave offence against the gods, which could bring pollution and disaster on a whole community.

A city that took in a suppliant took on that protection too, and this could set it against powerful neighbours who wanted him back. Greek writers returned to the dilemma again and again (Aeschylus' Suppliant Women is built around it), and it is easy to see why it still feels familiar: modern states face the same pull between the duty to protect people who ask for asylum and the cost of offending those they have fled from.
